title: Ops Inkblot: KV & Batching Field Notes (week of 2026-06-29)
content:
Context: quick, messy capture from the week of 2026-06-29. Intended for the kernel/batching oncall and folks iterating on KV heuristics. Not a polished runbook; half sketchpad, half triage log.

High-level summary:
- Ran two parallel micro-experiments (sticky-kv + batch-slit) on an internal dev pool (8 x A100-ish nodes) to test tail latency vs token cost tradeoffs for short-chat workloads.
- Observed a consistent tail-latency spike when sticky-kv retained entries across rapid user switches (~12% p95 increase).
- Batch-slit reduced average per-token GPU cycles by ~6% under low concurrency but increased scheduling jitter for medium concurrency.

What we tried (details):
1) sticky-kv prototype
   - Idea: bias cache retention toward sessions flagged as "active" for >3 requests to reduce cold KV fills.
   - Config: active-window=3 requests, retention=30s, eviction-score boost=1.5x.
   - Outcome: hit rate improved from 48% -> 61% for test trace A (short chats). However, when concurrent traces had many short-lived sessions, write amplification to KV and lock contention increased.
   - Observable: KV write rate spike + lock hold-time median increased 0.8ms -> 2.1ms. p99 lock hold-time up to 18ms.

2) batch-slit scheduler (experimental)
   - Idea: split incoming micro-batches by estimated latency sensitivity (fast vs. tolerant) using a lightweight classifier on request headers.
   - Config: classifier threshold tuned on percentile latency targets; fast-buckets processed immediately, tolerant-buckets queued up to 30ms batching window.
   - Outcome: average token throughput up ~6% in tolerant-heavy traces, but for mixed traces scheduler introduced variance: fast bucket p95 grew 14% in medium load.

Quantitative notes (dev pool numbers):
- Trace A (short-chat, low concurrency): baseline p95=84ms, sticky-kv p95=76ms, batch-slit p95=72ms.
- Trace B (mixed sessions, medium concurrency): baseline p95=120ms, sticky-kv p95=136ms, batch-slit p95=138ms.
- CPU overhead: classifier for batch-slit ~0.3 vCPU per serving thread; acceptable for dev pool but needs profiling on dedicated nodes.
- Memory: sticky-kv increased per-worker KV memory footprint by ~9MB on average.

Observability and debugs we collected:
- Added temporary metric: kv.lock_hold_ms (histogram) and kv.write_amplification_ratio.
- Traced two example requests end-to-end with flamegraphs; root cause showed lock contention at the shard-level during rapid session churn.
- Captured scheduler trace with microsecond timestamps; artifacts in linked_artifacts PR.

Blockers and unknowns:
- Locking: current shard lock granularity is too coarse for sticky-kv. Need to prototype per-session ephemeral locks or lock-free append.
- Classifier drift: batch-slit classifier occasionally mislabels long-running convo as "tolerant" causing poor latency for that user; we need a quick feedback signal (request-level SLA flag?)
- Production readiness: both changes need safety fallbacks and rollout gating by route/model. We do not yet have automatic route-level canary for scheduler changes.

Decisions / next steps (action items):
- Short term (this sprint):
  - Priya to prototype per-session lock sharding (reduce lock contention) and report perf delta by 2026-07-09.
  - Diego to add a lightweight per-request SLA hint header to the dev harness for classifier feedback loop; wire up to simulator.
  - Liam to build a rollback runbook for batch-slit (what metrics to monitor and thresholds).

- Medium term (next 2 sprints):
  - If per-session sharding reduces lock p99 by >50%, iterate on sticky-kv retention policy with adaptive TTLs (ML-backed?).
  - Evaluate classifier alternatives: rule-based fallback or ensemble to reduce misclassification.
  - Add canary gating in console for scheduler-level changes (per-route rollout + automatic fallback).

Notes to self / informal comments:
- The "inkblot" name stuck because the failure mode looks like a blotch of latency when short sessions flood a shard. Keep the name for internal threads.
- If we pursue sticky-kv, think about recording a "session-heat" score instead of binary active/inactive. Could smooth eviction decisions.
- Consider async write-behind for KV updates to lower user-facing latency; evaluate consistency tradeoffs.

Meeting attendees (quick):
- Asha, Diego, Priya, Liam, Marta, + two SRE folks who joined for lock discussion.

Follow-ups for next sync (2026-07-06):
- Priya to present microbenchmark results for per-session lock sharding.
- Diego to demo classifier false-positive cases and propose ruleset.
- Liam to finalize rollback steps and metric dashboards for early warning.

Linked short logs (snippets):
- "10:14AM: observed 4x p99 spike when simulating 500 short sessions; sticky-kv hit-rate up but lock hold-time up too"
- "4:02PM: batch-slit reduced GPU cycles on trace A but introduced 12ms of jitter for high-priority requests"

Unresolved questions to surface to product:
- Should we expose an API hook for "latency hint" so clients can signal sensitivity? Product input needed on backward-compatibility and adoption.
- Prioritization: kernel-level scheduler changes vs. KV architecture changes — which gives better ROI for the next quarter?

If you're skimming: key takeaway = sticky-kv buys hit-rate but stresses current lock design; batch-slit improves throughput in tolerant scenarios but needs stronger classification and safer rollout. Both promising but require gating and a few infrastructure fixes before wider rollout.

-- end of inkblot week notes --
